lessons.title: Sound Creation for Media
lessons.description: The forms of media that use created sounds and the six types of sound creation.
lessons.content_html:
Why Sound Creation Matters

Sound creation is the process of producing audio specifically designed for use in media. Without carefully created sound, a film would feel flat, a video game would lack immersion, and an advertisement would fail to grab attention. Understanding the different forms of media and types of sound creation is the starting point for this unit.

Forms of Media Using Sound Creation

Sound creation is used across a wide range of media. Each form has its own requirements, but all rely on carefully designed audio to enhance the audience’s experience.

Key Fact

The ten forms of media you must know are: radio broadcasts, movies, TV shows, video games, advertisements, jingles, podcasts, animations, theatre, and installations.

Radio broadcasts rely entirely on sound — music, speech, and effects must tell the whole story without any visual support. Movies and TV shows use sound to build atmosphere, convey emotion, and guide the viewer’s attention. Video games require interactive sound that responds to the player’s actions in real time.

Advertisements use short, punchy sound design to make products memorable. A jingle is a specific type of sound creation — a brief, catchy tune designed to stick in the listener’s mind and associate with a product or brand.

Podcasts use voice recording, music beds, and effects to create engaging audio-only content. Animations need all sounds to be created from scratch because there is no live-action audio to capture. Theatre uses live and pre-recorded sound effects and music to support performances. Installations are immersive art or exhibition spaces that use sound to create an environment or atmosphere for visitors.

Types of Sound Creation

There are six main types of sound creation. Each serves a different purpose within a media production.

Foley

Foley is the art of creating realistic, everyday sounds in a studio. Foley artists watch the visual footage and perform the sounds in sync — for example, walking on gravel to create footstep sounds, or crumpling paper to simulate fire. These sounds are recorded and layered into the final production to make it feel real.

Ambience

Ambience (also called atmosphere or room tone) is the background sound that sets the scene. It tells the audience where and when the action takes place. A busy city street has traffic and voices. A forest has birdsong and rustling leaves. Without ambience, a scene feels unnaturally silent and disconnected.

Dialogue

Dialogue is recorded speech between characters. In film and TV, dialogue is captured on set using boom microphones and lavalier mics, then cleaned and balanced in post-production. If on-set recording is unusable, actors re-record their lines in a studio — a process called ADR (Automated Dialogue Replacement).

Voice-overs

A voice-over is a piece of narration or commentary recorded separately and placed over the visuals. Voice-overs are common in documentaries, advertisements, trailers, and podcasts. The voice-over artist does not appear on screen — they provide information, set the tone, or guide the audience’s understanding.

Underscore

An underscore is background music that supports the visuals without drawing attention to itself. It sits beneath the dialogue and action, reinforcing the mood of a scene. A tense underscore might use sustained low strings, while a romantic underscore might feature gentle piano. The audience may not consciously notice the underscore, but it shapes how they feel about what they are watching.

Key Fact

The six types of sound creation are: Foley (recreated everyday sounds), ambience (background environment sounds), dialogue (character speech), voice-overs (off-screen narration), underscore (background music for mood), and spot effects (specific one-off sounds synced to events).

Spot Effects

Spot effects are individual sound effects that are timed precisely to a specific on-screen event. A gunshot, a car horn, a doorbell, or a glass smashing are all spot effects. Unlike ambience (which is continuous), a spot effect is a one-off sound triggered at an exact moment. Spot effects can be sourced from effects libraries, created using Foley techniques, or synthesised digitally.

Imagine a scene in a thriller where a detective enters a dark warehouse. The ambience includes distant traffic and a low hum from overhead lights. Foley provides the detective’s echoing footsteps on concrete. A tense underscore builds with sustained cello. The detective speaks into a radio — this is dialogue. A narrator describes the scene — this is a voice-over. A door slams shut behind them — this is a spot effect. All six types work together to create a convincing, immersive experience.

Key Fact

Foley and spot effects are different. Foley recreates everyday, continuous sounds performed in sync with visuals (e.g. footsteps, clothing rustle). Spot effects are single, precisely timed events (e.g. an explosion, a phone ring). Foley is always performed live; spot effects may come from libraries, synthesis, or Foley.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to describe or explain types of sound creation, always give a specific example for each type. For instance, do not just write “Foley is everyday sounds” — write “Foley is the recreation of everyday sounds such as footsteps or door creaks, performed in sync with the visuals.” In extended response questions, explain how different sound types work together to create atmosphere in a specific media form.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sound creation is used across ten forms of media including movies, video games, radio, podcasts, theatre, and installations.
  • The six types of sound creation are Foley, ambience, dialogue, voice-overs, underscore, and spot effects — each serves a different purpose in a production.
  • In any media production, multiple types of sound creation are layered together to build a convincing and immersive audio experience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a sound designer might use different types of sound creation to build atmosphere in a horror video game.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis covering multiple sound types with clear links to how they create horror atmosphere. E.g. Dark, low-frequency ambience (wind, distant groaning) establishes unease. Foley footsteps on creaky floorboards make the player feel present. A tense underscore with dissonant strings builds dread. Spot effects like sudden door slams or screams create jump scares. Interactive sound design means these respond to player actions in real time, increasing immersion.
Mid band (3-4): Some analysis with at least two sound types linked to atmosphere, but less detailed.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about sound in games with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: Sound creation is used in many different forms of media. Choose two contrasting forms of media and discuss how the requirements for sound creation differ between them. Refer to specific types of sound creation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion of two clearly contrasting media forms with specific references to sound creation types. E.g. Compares film (uses all six types: Foley, ambience, dialogue, voice-over, underscore, spot effects, all pre-mixed for fixed playback) with video games (requires interactive/adaptive sound that responds to player actions, ambience must loop seamlessly, spot effects must trigger dynamically). Well-structured with clear reasoning.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good comparison with several specific examples but less detailed analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about two media forms but limited comparison or fewer specific types referenced.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about sound in media with little comparison.

lessons.title: Methods of Sound Creation
lessons.description: Physical props, environmental sounds, synthesis, sampling and effects libraries.
lessons.content_html:
Five Methods of Sound Creation

Once you know what types of sound are needed for a production, you need to understand how those sounds are made. There are five main methods of sound creation, ranging from entirely physical techniques to fully digital processes. A professional sound designer will use a combination of all five to build a complete soundtrack.

Method 1: Physical Props

Physical props are real objects used to create sounds. This method is at the heart of Foley work. The process involves two stages: creation of props (finding or building suitable objects) and capture and editing of audio (recording the sounds and processing them to fit the production).

For example, to create the sound of walking on snow, a Foley artist might squeeze a bag of cornflour. To simulate breaking bones, they might snap celery sticks. The sound is recorded using a close-placement microphone, then edited — trimmed, EQ’d, and time-aligned to the visual.

Key Fact

The five methods of sound creation are: physical props (creation of props, capture and editing of audio), environmental sounds (capture in different environments, selection and editing), sound synthesis (creation of patches, waveform selection, filters, modifiers), digital sample manipulation (import of audio, mapping, looping), and effects libraries (commercial, online, DAW loops).

Method 2: Environmental Sounds

Environmental sounds are recorded on location rather than in a studio. The process involves capture in different environments — such as a forest, a busy street, or an empty church — and then selection and editing of the best recordings. A sound recordist uses a portable recorder and specialised microphones to capture the natural soundscape of a location.

These recordings are used primarily for ambience tracks. After recording, the sound designer listens through hours of material, selects the most useful sections, removes unwanted noise, and edits the clips to loop seamlessly in the final production.

Method 3: Sound Synthesis

Sound synthesis creates sounds entirely from electronic signals. It is used when a sound designer needs a tone, texture, or effect that does not exist in the real world. The process begins with creation of patches — a patch is a saved set of synthesiser settings that produces a particular sound.

Waveform selection is the starting point. Common waveforms include sine (smooth, pure tone), sawtooth (bright, buzzy), square (hollow, reed-like), and triangle (soft, flute-like). Each waveform has a different timbre.

Filters shape the sound by removing certain frequencies. A low-pass filter removes high frequencies, making the sound warmer. A high-pass filter removes low frequencies, making the sound thinner. Adjusting the filter cutoff changes how bright or dark the sound appears.

Modifiers add movement and expression. An LFO (Low Frequency Oscillator) creates slow, repeating changes — for example, a gentle wobble in pitch (vibrato) or volume (tremolo). An envelope controls how a sound changes over time using four stages: Attack (how quickly the sound reaches full volume), Decay (how quickly it drops to the sustain level), Sustain (the level held while a key is pressed), and Release (how quickly the sound fades after the key is released). Together these form the ADSR envelope.

Method 4: Digital Sample Manipulation

Digital sample manipulation starts with a real recording (a sample) and transforms it into something new. The process involves creation of patches (building a playable instrument from samples), import of audio (loading recordings into a sampler), mapping (assigning different samples to different keys on a keyboard so that pitch, velocity, or zone varies), and looping (setting a section of audio to repeat seamlessly so a short sample can sustain indefinitely).

For example, a sound designer might record a single violin note, import it into a sampler, map it across the keyboard at different pitches, add a loop point so it sustains, and then apply filters and effects. The result is a playable virtual violin built from a single real recording.

Method 5: Effects Libraries

An effects library is a collection of pre-recorded sounds organised by category — footsteps, weather, vehicles, animals, impacts, and so on. There are three main sources:

  • Commercial libraries — professionally recorded collections sold by specialist companies. These offer high-quality, royalty-free sounds.
  • Online libraries — free or subscription-based websites offering downloadable effects. Quality varies, and licensing terms must be checked.
  • DAW loops — built-in sound libraries that come with Digital Audio Workstations like Logic Pro, Ableton Live, or GarageBand. These include both effects and musical loops.
Key Fact

The ADSR envelope controls how a synthesised or sampled sound changes over time. Attack = time to reach full volume. Decay = time to drop to the sustain level. Sustain = the volume held while the key is pressed. Release = time for the sound to fade after the key is released. Changing these values dramatically alters the character of the sound.

The method a sound designer chooses depends on the production’s needs, budget, and deadlines. Physical props and environmental recording give the most realistic results but take the most time. Sound synthesis is ideal for sci-fi, electronic, or abstract sounds that don’t exist in the real world. Digital sample manipulation offers a middle ground — starting from a real recording but shaping it into something new. Effects libraries are the fastest option but offer less originality. Most productions use a combination of all five methods.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing methods of sound creation, be specific about the process. For synthesis questions, always mention the key building blocks: waveform selection, filters, and modifiers (LFO and envelope/ADSR). For sample manipulation, mention import, mapping, and looping. Strong answers show precise technical vocabulary over vague descriptions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five methods of sound creation are physical props, environmental sounds, sound synthesis, digital sample manipulation, and effects libraries.
  • Sound synthesis uses waveforms, filters, and modifiers (LFO and ADSR envelope) to create sounds electronically.
  • Digital sample manipulation transforms real recordings into playable instruments through import, mapping, and looping.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of using physical props compared to effects libraries for sound creation in a film production.

practice_questions.text: A sound designer is creating audio for a science fiction video game that features alien environments and futuristic weapons. Discuss which methods of sound creation would be most appropriate and how they would be used. Refer to at least three methods in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:

Digital sample manipulation could transform real recordings (e.g. a recorded metal clang) into alien sounds through extreme pitch shifting and looping. Environmental recording could capture industrial ambiences as a base for alien landscapes. Effects libraries provide quick access to generic sci-fi elements. Well-structured with specific technical detail.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with three methods and some technical detail.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about two or more methods but less specific to the sci-fi context.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about sound creation with little application to the scenario.

lessons.title: Arranging & Exporting Sounds
lessons.description: DAW arrangement tools, diegetic vs non-diegetic sound, and export formats.
lessons.content_html:
Arranging Sounds in a DAW

Once sounds have been created, they need to be arranged into a complete soundtrack that fits the visual media. This is done inside a DAW (Digital Audio Workstation). The arrangement stage is where individual sounds — Foley, ambience, dialogue, underscore, and spot effects — are placed, timed, and balanced against each other.

DAW Arrangement Tools

Modern DAWs provide a powerful set of tools for arranging sounds to picture. You must know the following arrangement tools:

Video file import — the DAW can import a video file so the sound designer sees the visuals directly in the timeline. This allows precise synchronisation of audio to picture.

Audio import — pre-recorded audio files (field recordings, effects library sounds, dialogue takes) are imported into the project and placed on tracks in the timeline.

MIDI import — MIDI data from external sources can be imported and assigned to virtual instruments within the DAW, allowing synthesised sounds to be arranged alongside audio.

Audio and MIDI editing — clips can be cut, moved, copied, trimmed, faded, time-stretched, and pitch-shifted. MIDI notes can be quantised (snapped to a grid), transposed, or velocity-edited.

Layering — multiple sounds are stacked on separate tracks to build a rich, complex soundtrack. For example, a storm scene might layer wind ambience, rain Foley, thunder spot effects, and a tense underscore across four or more tracks.

Automation — Automation records parameter changes over time — for example, gradually fading the ambience volume down as dialogue begins, or sweeping a filter across a synthesised pad. Automation lanes are drawn directly onto tracks.

Markers — reference points placed on the timeline to label important moments (e.g. “Car crash — 01:23”, “Dialogue starts — 02:05”). Markers help the sound designer navigate a long project and ensure key events are hit precisely.

Key Fact

The six DAW arrangement tools you must know are: video file import, audio/MIDI import, audio/MIDI editing, layering, automation, and markers. Each plays a specific role in building a synchronised soundtrack.

Tempo Changes

Tempo changes are used when the pace of the music needs to match changes in the visual action. A chase scene might require an accelerating tempo, while a reflective moment might need a gradual slowing down. In a DAW, tempo changes can be programmed into the tempo map, and all MIDI tracks automatically follow the new tempo.

Sound Arrangement Concepts

Arranging sounds for media is not just about timing — it involves creative decisions about how sounds work together to support the visual story.

Texture refers to how many layers of sound are present and how they interact. A thin texture (one or two sounds) creates a sense of isolation or stillness. A thick texture (many layered sounds) creates richness or chaos.

Mood is the emotional feeling the soundtrack creates. Major keys and warm timbres suggest happiness; minor keys and dissonant harmonies suggest tension or sadness. The sound designer chooses and arranges sounds to match the intended mood of each scene.

Style refers to the genre or aesthetic of the soundtrack. A period drama might use orchestral underscore, while a modern thriller might use electronic textures and processed effects.

Impact is the power or force of a sound moment. High-impact sounds (a loud explosion, a sudden musical hit) grab the audience’s attention. Low-impact sounds (a quiet ambient wash) sit in the background. Contrast between high and low impact creates drama.

Diegetic vs Non-Diegetic Sound

One of the most important concepts in sound arrangement for media is the distinction between diegetic and non-diegetic sound.

Diegetic sound comes from within the world of the story. The characters can hear it. Examples include dialogue between characters, a radio playing music in a room, traffic outside a window, or a phone ringing. Diegetic sound helps establish the reality of the scene.

Non-diegetic sound exists outside the story world. Only the audience hears it. Examples include underscore music, voice-over narration, and dramatic sound effects added for impact. Non-diegetic sound guides the audience’s emotions without the characters being aware of it.

Key Fact

Diegetic sound = characters can hear it (dialogue, a TV in the room, footsteps). Non-diegetic sound = only the audience hears it (underscore, voice-over, dramatic effects). Some sounds can shift between the two — for example, music playing on a character’s headphones (diegetic) that transitions into a full orchestral arrangement (non-diegetic).

Exporting the Final Audio

Once the arrangement is complete, the final step is exporting. The sound designer must choose the correct format for the intended use:

MP4 — a compressed video format widely used for web and mobile delivery. Audio is embedded within the video file.

MOV — Apple’s video format, commonly used in professional video editing workflows. Supports high-quality codecs.

MP3 — a compressed audio format. Smaller file size but some quality is lost due to lossy compression. Suitable for podcasts, web audio, and drafts.

WAV — an uncompressed audio format. Full quality with no data loss, but large file sizes. Industry standard for professional delivery.

AIF (AIFF) — Apple’s uncompressed audio format. Equivalent quality to WAV, used mainly on Mac systems.

The final process is the render of audio to video — combining the finished audio mix with the video file into a single exported media file. The DAW or video editing software bounces (exports) the audio and embeds it into the video container (MP4 or MOV).

Key Fact

Compressed formats: MP3 (audio, lossy), MP4 (video, compressed), MOV (video, compressed). Uncompressed formats: WAV (audio, full quality), AIF (audio, full quality). Always use WAV or AIF for professional delivery; MP3 for web or draft use.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions about diegetic and non-diegetic sound, always give specific examples from a named media form. Do not just define the terms — explain how each type contributes to the audience’s experience. For export format questions, state whether the format is compressed or uncompressed and explain why that matters for the intended use.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • DAW arrangement tools include video import, audio/MIDI import and editing, layering, automation, and markers — all essential for synchronising sound to picture.
  • Diegetic sound comes from within the story world (characters hear it); non-diegetic sound is only heard by the audience (underscore, voice-over).
  • Export formats include compressed (MP3, MP4, MOV) and uncompressed (WAV, AIF) — the choice depends on the intended delivery platform and quality requirements.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of non-diegetic sound?
A) A character speaking to another character
B) A radio playing in the background of a scene
C) Orchestral music played to create tension for the audience

practice_questions.text: Identify two uncompressed audio export formats.
Describe how a sound designer would use automation and markers when arranging a soundtrack in a DAW.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per valid point (max 3): Automation records parameter changes over time (1), e.g. fading volume or sweeping a filter (1). Markers are reference points on the timeline labelling key moments (1), e.g. 'car crash at 01:23' (1). Both help synchronise audio precisely to the visuals (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between diegetic and non-diegetic sound, using examples from a film or TV production.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explanation with examples (max 4): Diegetic sound comes from within the story world and characters can hear it (1), e.g. dialogue or a radio playing (1). Non-diegetic sound exists outside the story and only the audience hears it (1), e.g. underscore music or voice-over narration (1). Some sounds can transition between the two (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the DAW arrangement tools of layering and automation could be used together to create a convincing storm scene in a film soundtrack.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis showing both tools working together. E.g. Layering: place wind ambience on track 1, rain Foley on track 2, thunder spot effects on track 3, and tense underscore on track 4. Each layer adds depth and realism. Automation: gradually increase the rain volume as the storm builds, automate a low-pass filter on the wind to make it more intense, fade the underscore in slowly to build tension. Automation allows the soundtrack to evolve dynamically rather than staying static.
Mid band (3-4): Some valid points about both tools but less detailed.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about layering or automation with limited application.

practice_questions.text: A client has asked you to create a soundtrack for a short animated film that will be shown online and at a film festival. Discuss the arrangement and export decisions you would need to make, explaining why format selection matters for different delivery platforms.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion covering arrangement (layering, automation, tempo changes, markers for key scenes, diegetic vs non-diegetic choices) and export (WAV/AIF for festival projection — uncompressed, full quality; MP4/MP3 for online — compressed, smaller files for streaming). Explains why different platforms need different formats. Well-structured.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion covering arrangement and export with some justification.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points about arrangement or export but limited connection between platform and format.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about arrangement or export with little reasoning.

glossary_terms.definition: Digital Audio Workstation — software such as Logic Pro, Ableton Live, or Pro Tools used for recording, editing, mixing, and mastering audio.
Musical Instrument Digital Interface — a protocol that allows electronic instruments and computers to exchange performance data such as note, velocity, and duration.
The process of recording parameter changes over time within a DAW, such as gradual volume fades or filter sweeps, so they play back automatically.
The speed of a piece of music, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
Sound that originates from within the world of the story — characters can hear it. Examples include dialogue, a radio playing, or a car horn.
Sound that exists outside the world of the story — only the audience hears it. Examples include underscore, voice-over narration, and dramatic sound effects.
The file type and encoding used to save audio or video, each with different quality, compression, and compatibility characteristics.
